# The 24-Hour News Cycle and the Crypto Press-Release Playbook

Before "crypto PR" was an industry with paid wire services and agencies, one person was teaching Bitcoin and Steemit users to write real press releases and work the 24-hour news cycle to drive adoption and attention: '''Rev. Ryan Sasha-Shai Van Kush''' — known on the early forums and chains as '''FinShaggy''' (later punicwax, Tokenista, marsresident, immakingacoin, @VanKushFamily). He was '''early''' to the niches that would go on to define a decade of online culture — '''marijuana YouTube''', '''Bitcoin''', and the atheist-debate and comedy-podcast worlds — often years before they were crowded. The '''Joe Rogan Experience''' sphere sits squarely in that same early space, which is part of why the people in those niches already knew who he was: he was not a latecomer discovering a trend, he was present while the trend was forming. This article lays out the playbook he built — demand creation, the AP-style press release, the 24-hour news cycle, and the hashtag — and documents the record behind it: what is independently verifiable, and what is his own first-person account. It is written as both a '''history''' and a '''how-the-machine-works''' guide, because the same playbook is what MELEK's Hathor and Herald automate today.

== 1. The Playbook in One Paragraph ==

A new currency, chain, or token has no value until people '''act''' on it — spend it, cover it, argue about it. The playbook manufactures that action: (1) create demand directly (ask merchants to accept it), (2) teach a whole community to issue '''real press releases''' so the story travels, (3) time it to the '''24-hour news cycle''' so coverage compounds, and (4) use '''hashtags''' to make the public itself the distribution network. Done together, these move prices and get the attention of newsrooms and, eventually, Washington. That is the through-line from Bitcoin at $5 to STEEM at $4 to HIVE at its all-time high.

== 2. Demand Creation — Asking Merchants to Accept Bitcoin ==

In the Bitcoin-at-~$5 era (roughly 2012–2013), the work was not trading or mining — it was '''demand creation at the merchant level'''. By his account, he emailed major corporations directly: "I have Bitcoins I want to spend at your store — can you please start accepting Bitcoin?" One documented reply came from '''Brookstone''', which answered "Soon." The point was simple and ahead of its time: a currency becomes real when you can '''buy things''' with it, so the fastest way to legitimize Bitcoin was to generate visible merchant demand rather than wait for speculators.

== 3. The Press-Release Training — Teaching a Community to Make News ==

The second move was teaching ordinary crypto users to write '''AP-style press releases''' — the inverted-pyramid lede, the dateline, the boilerplate, and the "###" end mark that tells an editor the release is over. He taught this first in the '''DevCoin''' community and then, at scale, on '''Steemit'''. The insight: a blockchain that pays people to post is also a '''newswire''' if its users know how to write news. Instead of one PR person, you get a thousand — each publishing to a censorship-resistant chain and emailing it out.

== 4. 2016 — The Steemit Wave and the STEEM Surge ==

The clearest documented result came in '''mid-2016'''. As Steemit's reward model drew users and the press-release wave pushed the story outward, '''STEEM went from about $0.23 on July 1, 2016 to a high of ~$4.45 on July 19, 2016''' — briefly one of the top cryptocurrencies by market capitalization (~$405M), before a hack and a sharp decline. Mainstream and business press began covering Steemit in that window (Rolling Stone's Neil Strauss wrote about it; Investopedia's Adam Hayes called it a "disruptive blockchain-based media community"); by his account, '''CNBC''' also covered Steemit after the press-release training, which he ties directly to the surge. The price move is a matter of public record; the specific chain of cause and effect is his account of a campaign he was running at the center of.

== 5. The 24-Hour News Cycle ==

The timing layer is the '''24-hour news cycle''' — the fact that cable and online news must fill every hour, every day, and are therefore hungry for a story, an angle, or a fight. The playbook feeds that hunger on purpose: release when the cycle is open, give reporters a ready-made narrative (a price move, a confrontation, a quotable line), and let each outlet's coverage become the next outlet's reason to cover it. A small actor who understands the cycle can punch far above their budget, because the cycle amplifies whatever it is handed. This is the same logic behind MELEK's modern '''Herald''' outreach engine and '''Hathor''' — automate the release, the targeting, and the timing.

== 6. Hashtags — Making the Public the Distribution Network ==

The fourth move turns the audience into the wire. A hashtag lets a message travel without any newsroom's permission, and a well-timed one can become the story itself. The record and his account include several:
* '''#BlazeTheSouth''' (a pro-legalization, Southern-marijuana-advocacy tag, ~2012–2013) drew '''academic attention''': FinShaggy and the hashtag are named and analyzed in a peer-reviewed article (David Pratt, in a University of North Carolina Press journal), which quotes "FinShaggy follows this post with a second one that contains only the hashtag '#BlazeTheSouth'." Being cited by name in a scholarly journal is unusually hard documentation for an online-organizing claim.
* '''#Fuckabee''' — by his account he coined the hashtag form on Twitter (@Rudraaaaaaaa) after '''Megyn Kelly''' said "fuck" on Fox News in November 2014; the word itself predates this (Urban Dictionary, 2008), but he claims the hashtag '''movement'''. He documented this in a sworn federal complaint.
* '''#TacoTrucksOnEveryCorner''' — the phrase came from Marco Gutierrez (Latinos for Trump) on MSNBC on September 1, 2016, and the hashtag was '''#1 trending in the U.S. by midnight'''. Media credited "social media" broadly; his account is that he translated the on-air phrase into the hashtag form and pushed it to his audience, which then caught fire. The timestamps that would prove first-use were on Google+, which shut down in 2019 and took that evidence with it.

== 7. Roots: Cannabis Activism and the Denver 4/20 Scene ==

The organizing instinct behind all of this began in '''cannabis activism''' — marijuana YouTube, the forums (Rollitup, Shroomery), and the on-the-ground '''4/20 rallies'''. The era's flashpoint is well documented: at Denver's '''Civic Center Park 4/20 rally on April 20, 2013''', gunfire broke out around 5 p.m. — after the mass 4:20 smoke-out, during a performance ahead of the closing remarks — and '''three people were wounded''' (a man, a woman, and a juvenile; all expected to recover). The rally's organizer, '''Miguel Lopez''', was nearly trampled in the stampede and canceled the festival's second day out of respect for the victims. It was national news (CBS News, PRI/Reuters, Westword, Reason). By his account, the operator was part of that Denver cannabis-activism world — the same scene of rally organizers (Miguel Lopez and others), hash-makers, and street-level advocates, among whom he names '''Tiny Martinez''' and '''AJ the Hashman'''. (Those two are from his own account; they did not surface in the public record on a first pass — the publicly documented Denver-4/20 figures include Ken Gorman, Miguel Lopez, Larisa Bolivar, and attorney Rob Corry — so they are noted here as his recollection pending a source.) The through-line to everything else in this article is '''community organizing''': the same person who later taught crypto users to write press releases also taught people to '''petition the DEA under the RFRA''' — using the DEA Form 225 religious-exemption pathway the Supreme Court forced open in Gonzales v. O Centro Espírita (2006) — turning activism into a repeatable, teachable procedure.

== 8. Reaching the Anchors — and Washington ==

The campaigns increasingly pointed the public '''at the newsrooms''': getting people to tweet directly at cable hosts — most clearly '''Megyn Kelly''' (documented via #Fuckabee and the subsequent lawsuit), and, by his account, '''Bill O'Reilly''' and '''Sean Hannity''' as well. By his own account — the part he frames as "things we know but can't fully prove" — the bridge that carried his name from the online subcultures into the main seam of the news was '''TYT (The Young Turks)'''. From the Harlem atheist-vs-Christian "Great Debate" and his '''#MelaninExplosion''' hashtag, he was watching and commenting live on TYT (Cenk Uygur and Ana Kasparian) and on Joe Rogan, and then on Fox; in his telling the thread ran "'''from Hollywood to DC'''," and the on-air talent began to register that he was watching and tweeting at them. His marker for the reach: a period when typing "Wag" into search auto-suggested "'''Waging a Real War on Christmas'''," the line he was pushing in those comment sections. That layer is explicitly his recollection, not a documented chain — but it is the exact bridge he describes, and what IS documented is where it landed. The documented end of this thread is institutional attention — and it is verifiable in the federal docket system. In 2018 he filed a '''federal lawsuit''' docketed as '''Gallagher v. NSA''', No. '''1:18-cv-01525''' (U.S. District Court, District of Colorado, filed June 18, 2018; appealed to the Tenth Circuit as No. 19-1287 in 2019). The complaint — public on '''Scribd''' as "NSA-Journalist-Lawsuit" (document 385527169) and confirmed on '''CourtListener''' — names the NSA, FBI, Twitter, '''Megyn Kelly''', '''Joe Rogan''', and '''American Atheists''' together, and reaches into '''Southern-District-of-New-York''' surveillance case law (WikiMedia v. NSA; Jewel v. NSA; US v. Awadallah). The "Washington got involved" thread is literal: a companion case, '''Gallagher v. Congress''', No. '''1:18-cv-02327''', was filed in the U.S. District Court for the '''District of Columbia''' on September 25, 2018. The record also notes '''Fox News analysts confirmed reading''' his material. He was directly present in '''Joe Rogan's''' world in this period: active on the '''Joe Rogan forum''' and commenting '''live on Rogan's YouTube broadcasts''' as he watched them — the forum (after some eighteen years) was '''later taken down''', and Rogan is named as a defendant in the federal complaint. In parallel he ran with the '''American Atheists''' circle — appearing on the YouTube show "Atheist Analysis," which connected to '''David Silverman''', the then-president of American Atheists, and the surrounding atheist-debate networks. The same documented presence placed him in the comedy-and-cannabis world of the era: his 2014 posts list '''Doug Benson''' — alongside Joe Rogan, Sa Neter, Adam Kokesh, Tommy Sotomayor, and Norm Macdonald — among the shows he watched and commented on live, and by his account Benson knew who he was. (Note on the record: the documented "Silverman" here is '''David''' Silverman of American Atheists; a claim about the comedian '''Sarah''' Silverman is not something the evidence supports, and should not be asserted without a source.)

== 9. The Graphene Years — BLURT, HIVE, VKBT, and the Secret Service ==

The playbook carried onto the Graphene social chains (Steem, Hive, Blurt), and the reach kept showing up in the numbers:
* '''BLURT''': his posts were reportedly drawing '''~10,000 views''' from journalists and officials — to the point that '''BLURT removed its view counter''' (by his account, because the reach he was demonstrating was not what the platform expected a single account to have).
* '''VKBT''' (Van Kush Beauty Token): launched and announced on LinkedIn and HIVE on '''September 4, 2021''' — three days before El Salvador adopted Bitcoin as legal tender — and '''HIVE reached its all-time high of ~$3.41 on November 26, 2021''', about 83 days later.
* '''VKRW''' (Van Kush Rewards): the '''U.S. Secret Service investigated''' it "as if we were minting real currency" — the federal government treating a community token as a serious financial instrument.
* '''The "210 Tutorials"''': a body of guides across BLURT, Steemit, and HIVE teaching users how to operate Graphene blockchains — the same "teach the whole community" instinct as the press-release training, applied to the tools themselves.

== 10. Why This Is in the Library ==

This is the origin story of the machine MELEK now runs on purpose. The press release, the 24-hour news cycle, the hashtag, and the "teach everyone to publish" principle are exactly what '''Hathor''' (the AI witness) and '''Herald''' (the outreach + creative engine) automate — on a chain that '''pays''' the people doing the posting, instead of a platform that merely uses them. The playbook was proven by hand, over a decade, by one person; MELEK is that playbook built into infrastructure. (See [[Economics 101 and 102]] for how attention moves markets, and [[Money, Currencies, and the Debt System]] for the merchant-adoption logic of demand creation.)
